instructional_purpose: Teaches the construction in which a noun stands before a verb that already carries an object pronoun coreferential with that noun, and shows the learner how to decide what case the pre-posed noun takes and what is taken to govern it.
concepts_taught: preoccupation construction (الاشتغال)
returning pronoun (الضمير العائد) as the element actually filling the verb's object slot
difference between bare object pre-posing and pre-posing with a resumptive pronoun
accusative assigned by an estimated deleted verb rather than by the visible verb
environments in which the pre-posed noun is instead nominative as a topic
gender and number agreement of the returning pronoun with the pre-posed noun
non-human plural agreement resolving to a feminine singular pronoun
topic-comment discourse effect and its use in listing successive actions

linguistic_propositions.proposition: If a verb bears an object pronoun that refers back to a noun standing before it, the verb's object position is already filled, so the visible verb is not what assigns case to that noun.
The accusative on the pre-posed noun is licensed by a verb that is estimated and unpronounced, semantically matching the visible verb.
The accusative is the preferred case whenever the visible verb is of a type that could have taken the pre-posed noun as a direct object.
A particle standing before the pre-posed noun that cannot be followed by an accusative forces the nominative, the noun then being a topic of a nominal sentence.
Conditional particles specifically require the nominative on the pre-posed noun.
The topic marker أمّا is followed by a nominative pre-posed noun.
The returning pronoun must match the pre-posed noun in gender and number, with non-human plurals taking the feminine singular clitic.
Case selection in this construction is a two-way choice between accusative and nominative.
The pre-posed noun is semantically the undergoer even where it is analysed syntactically as a topic; the agent remains the verb's own subject.

recognition_criteria: a noun precedes a finite verb instead of following it
the verb carries an attached object pronoun
that pronoun has no antecedent other than the pre-posed noun
removing the pronoun would leave the verb needing exactly that noun as its complement
the pre-posed noun is not itself the agent of the verb
procedures: locate the noun standing before the verb
locate the clitic pronoun on the verb and confirm it refers back to that noun
ask whether the verb is of a type that could govern the noun directly as an object
scan leftward for a particle that constrains what may follow it
assign accusative when nothing blocks it and name the estimated governor, or nominative when a preceding particle demands a nominal opening
select the clitic that matches the noun in gender and number
conditions: there must be an overt pronoun on the verb linking back to the pre-posed noun
the verb must be able in principle to take the pre-posed noun as an argument for the accusative reading
nothing in the left periphery may block an accusative opening
exceptions: after the topic marker meaning as-for, the pre-posed noun surfaces as nominative
non-human plural antecedents break the expected human-plural clitic pattern and take the feminine singular
the lesson also allows a topic analysis of the pre-posed noun even where it presents the accusative as the default
contrasts: bare pre-posing without a pronoun versus pre-posing with a pronoun
canonical verb-first order versus either pre-posed order
emphasis on a single element versus a full topic-comment partition
the visible verb as governor versus an estimated unpronounced governor

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating a pre-posed noun with a resumptive pronoun and one without as the same construction with the same analysis.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Both are well formed, but only one has its object slot already filled, so the two differ in what governs the pre-posed noun.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check for the clitic on the verb before deciding what assigns case to the pre-posed noun.

common_mistakes.pattern: Selecting a human masculine plural clitic for a non-human plural antecedent.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Non-human plurals control feminine singular agreement in the standard language.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Resolve the antecedent's animacy first, then choose the clitic.

common_mistakes.pattern: Keeping the accusative on the pre-posed noun after a particle that opens a nominal clause.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The particle constrains what may immediately follow it and so overrides the default case pattern.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Inspect the left periphery before assigning case.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading the pre-posed noun as the agent of the verb.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The agent is carried by the verb's own inflection or an independent subject; the pre-posed noun corresponds to the pronoun on the verb.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Match the pre-posed noun to the clitic, not to the subject inflection.

misleading_shortcuts: treating the mere presence of a clitic as proof of this construction without checking coreference
assuming the pre-posed noun is always accusative
assuming the case decision is binary when the tradition grades outcomes as obligatory, preferred or equally admissible
assuming any noun placed before a verb yields a topic-comment reading

instructional_purpose: Teaches the configuration in which two coordinated verbs both stand before a single noun that each of them could take as an argument, and presents the two classical schools' opposing rules for deciding which verb governs it and which is left with a pronoun.
concepts_taught: contention over a shared argument (التنازع)
the three-part structure of two governors plus one disputed noun
the Basran rule favouring the nearer, second verb
the Kufan rule favouring the earlier, first verb
resumptive pronoun on the losing verb as the resolution device
contention over arguments other than the direct object
agreement of the resolving pronoun with the shared noun

linguistic_propositions.proposition: When two coordinated verbs precede a single noun each could take as an argument, only one of them can be said to govern it.
One school assigns government to the verb nearer the noun on grounds of proximity.
The other school assigns government to the earlier verb on grounds of precedence in mention.
Both analyses describe well-formed usage and neither is to be treated as an error.
The verb that does not govern the shared noun is supplied with a pronoun coreferential with it.
The Kufan analysis can be displayed by rewriting the string as two successive clauses, the first with the overt noun and the second with a pronoun.
The pronoun may simply be left unexpressed whenever the sense is clear.
Contention may hold over a shared subject or over a shared prepositional complement as well as over a shared object, with the same school split applying.
The resolving pronoun must agree with the shared noun in gender and number.

recognition_criteria: two or more finite verbs stand before a single noun
the verbs are typically joined by the coordinating conjunction
each verb is independently capable of taking that noun in the same role
there is only one overt candidate noun for two argument slots
no second noun intervenes that could satisfy the first verb
procedures: confirm that both verbs precede the disputed noun
confirm that each verb could take that noun in the relevant role
choose an analysis: nearer verb governs, or earlier verb governs
leave the governing verb with the overt noun in the case that verb assigns
supply the non-governing verb with a pronoun agreeing with the shared noun in gender and number
state which analysis was adopted rather than presenting it as the only one
conditions: there must be two or more governors preceding the shared noun
the shared noun must be a plausible argument of each governor
the resolving pronoun must be selected by the features of the shared noun, not of either subject
exceptions: the pronoun is presented as omissible where context recovers it
contention is not limited to the object role and can involve a subject or a prepositional complement
where each verb receives its own explicit argument, the configuration is no longer one of contention
contrasts: contention against ordinary coordination in which each verb has its own distinct argument
contention against the preoccupation construction: two governors and one noun versus one governor and a displaced noun
the nearer-verb analysis against the earlier-verb analysis
an unresolved string against a string in which pronouns make the analysis explicit

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating one of the two school analyses as ungrammatical.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Both patterns are attested and each school defends its own; the disagreement is over preference, not over well-formedness.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Report the analysis chosen and keep the alternative attributed rather than suppressed.

common_mistakes.pattern: Choosing a resolving pronoun whose gender or number does not match the shared noun.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The pronoun stands in for the shared noun and inherits its features.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Copy gender and number from the shared noun, not from the nearer subject.

common_mistakes.pattern: Labelling ordinary coordination with two distinct objects as contention.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Contention requires competition for one and the same noun; two separate arguments leave nothing to dispute.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Count the overt argument nouns before applying the label.

common_mistakes.pattern: Insisting that an explicit resolving pronoun is always required.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The construction is presented as well formed with the pronoun left unexpressed when the sense is recoverable.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Treat the explicit pronoun as a disambiguating option rather than a formal requirement.

misleading_shortcuts: reading the second-verb rule as a universal default and discarding the rival analysis
rewriting the string into two sequential clauses, which removes the very configuration of two governors preceding one noun and therefore no longer displays contention
generalising the freedom to leave the pronoun unexpressed from object contention to subject contention, where an unexpressed subject pronoun is not equally available
treating the choice between the analyses as a matter of style only, when the two assign case and coreference differently

instructional_purpose: Teaches that an interrogative or negative particle standing between a mental-state verb and its expected complement blocks that verb from assigning case across it, so the following clause keeps its own internal case pattern.
concepts_taught: suspension of governance (التعليق)
the class of mental-state verbs (أفعال القلوب) and their double-accusative frame
interrogative particles as suspending elements
negative particles as suspending elements
retention of the embedded clause's own nominative pattern under suspension
the head-of-clause priority of the suspending particles as the stated explanation
the complementiser أنّ as a non-suspending element
the difference between an embedded question and a standalone question

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Mental-state verbs of knowing, supposing and considering take two accusative complements in their basic frame.
An interrogative or negative particle intervening between such a verb and its complement prevents the verb from assigning accusative case across it.
Under suspension the following clause keeps the case pattern it would have as an independent sentence.
The suspending set comprises the polar interrogatives هل and أ, the quantity word كم, the selector أيّ, the identity words مَن and ما, together with the negatives ما، لا، إنْ.
The complementiser أنّ does not suspend; the verb still takes the clause it heads as its complement, and أنّ itself assigns the accusative to the following noun.
Suspension is explained by the suspending particles' entitlement to stand at the head of their own clause, which claims the following material for themselves.
Within the suspended clause, the quantity interrogative assigns its own specification complement.
Suspension applies primarily to mental-state verbs and not to ordinary transitive verbs.
The verb still knows the content semantically while being unable to govern it syntactically.

recognition_criteria: the matrix verb belongs to the knowing, supposing or perceiving class
an interrogative or negative particle immediately follows that verb
the material after the particle is a complete clause with its own subject and predicate
the noun after the particle carries nominative rather than accusative marking
no accusative complement of the matrix verb is present
procedures: classify the matrix verb as a mental-state verb or not
check whether an interrogative or a negative particle immediately follows it
if such a particle is present, do not assign the verb's accusative frame to the following material
parse the following clause on its own internal terms
if the intervening element is the complementiser instead, restore the complement reading and let that complementiser assign accusative to its own subject
conditions: the matrix verb must be one that would otherwise take two accusative complements
the suspending particle must stand between the verb and the material it would otherwise govern
the following material must form a complete clause
exceptions: the complementiser is explicitly excluded from the suspending set
a question that is not embedded under a governing verb is not a case of suspension since there is no governance to block
ordinary transitive verbs are not subject to this phenomenon
contrasts: a mental-state verb with its plain double-accusative frame against the same verb followed by a suspending particle
a suspending interrogative against the non-suspending complementiser
an embedded question against a standalone question
suspension by an intervening particle against the two neighbouring phenomena of pronoun pre-emption and competing governors

common_mistakes.pattern: Classifying the complementiser meaning that among the suspending particles.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: That element introduces a complement the verb still takes, and it assigns accusative to its own subject.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Separate elements that head an independent clause from elements that package a clause as a complement.

common_mistakes.pattern: Forcing accusative endings onto the clause that follows a suspending particle.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The verb's case assignment does not cross the particle, so the clause keeps its own nominative subject and predicate.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Parse the post-particle clause independently before considering the matrix verb.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming every question word triggers suspension wherever it appears.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Suspension presupposes a governing verb whose assignment is being blocked; an independent question has no such governor.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Require an embedding mental-state verb before applying the label.

common_mistakes.pattern: Applying suspension to ordinary action verbs.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The phenomenon is stated for the mental-state class, whose complement frame is what gets blocked.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check the verb's class membership first.

misleading_shortcuts: treating the suspended clause as having no case relation to the matrix verb at all, when the tradition assigns the clause a position standing in for the blocked complements
reading the particle list as closed, when other head-of-clause elements are also treated as suspending in the wider tradition
inferring from the surface nominative that no governance relation exists anywhere in the structure
assuming a negative particle after a mental-state verb always suspends regardless of what it negates

instructional_purpose: Teaches that a mental-state verb placed after the material it would otherwise govern loses its accusative assignment, so that material stays a nominative sentence with the verb appended as a parenthetical comment.
concepts_taught: cancellation of governance by position (الإلغاء)
the three linear positions of a mental-state verb relative to its complements
obligatory assignment when the verb comes first

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A mental-state verb standing before both of its complements assigns accusative to both.
A mental-state verb standing between its two complements may either assign case or not, at the speaker's choice.
Assignment is the preferred option in the medial position.
A mental-state verb standing after both complements has its assignment cancelled obligatorily.
When assignment is cancelled the preceding material remains a nominal sentence of topic and predicate.
The explanation is that a governor reaches forward, so a verb arriving after its complements is too late to alter their case.
Cancellation is caused by linear position while suspension is caused by an intervening particle, and the two must not be conflated.
Only mental-state verbs undergo cancellation; a pre-posed object with an ordinary transitive verb belongs to the pronoun-pre-emption construction instead.
A trailing mental-state verb can follow a preceding verbal clause and still be analysed as cancelled.

recognition_criteria: the clause opens with a nominative topic and predicate
a mental-state verb follows that complete clause
the trailing verb carries first-person or other subject inflection of its own
no accusative marking appears on the preceding elements
no interrogative or negative particle separates the verb from the material
procedures: identify the mental-state verb and its linear position relative to the two complements
if the verb precedes both, apply the double-accusative frame
if the verb stands between them, choose either assignment or cancellation and apply it consistently to both elements
if the verb follows both, leave the preceding material in the nominative and read the verb as an appended comment
confirm that no particle is present, otherwise the case is one of suspension rather than cancellation
conditions: the verb must belong to the mental-state class
the two elements must be capable of forming a topic-predicate pair on their own
the case pattern must be applied uniformly rather than mixing accusative and nominative across the pair
exceptions: the medial position permits either outcome instead of fixing one
the phenomenon does not extend to ordinary transitive verbs
an intervening particle moves the analysis out of this phenomenon entirely

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating cancellation by position and blocking by an intervening particle as one phenomenon.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: One is triggered by the verb standing after its complements with no particle involved; the other by a particle standing between the verb and its complements.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check first for an intervening particle, then for the verb's linear position.

common_mistakes.pattern: Marking the preceding elements accusative when the verb comes last.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The elements have already taken their case as a nominal sentence and the later verb cannot reassign it.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Fix case by the structure available at the point the elements occur.

common_mistakes.pattern: Extending cancellation to ordinary transitive verbs.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The phenomenon is defined for the class whose frame is two accusative complements; a pre-posed object with an ordinary verb is a different construction.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Verify the verb's class before applying the label.

common_mistakes.pattern: Forgetting that the medial position permits both outcomes.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In that position the speaker may either apply or cancel assignment, and both are well formed.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Treat the medial position as a genuine choice and record which option was taken.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A pronoun object placed before its verb must appear in the detached accusative series rather than as a clitic.
Clitic pronouns cannot stand alone at the head of a clause and so cannot be pre-posed.
Placing the object before the verb narrows the action to that object to the exclusion of others.
The detached pronoun series distinguishes person, gender and number, including a dual member shared by both genders.
A pre-posed full noun may be echoed by a matching detached pronoun to make the exclusive reading explicit.
Pre-posing with a detached pronoun always implies exclusion of alternatives.
A restrictive particle, or negation followed by an exception, achieves the same restriction by other means.
The detached pronoun's person, gender and number must match its referent.
Ordinary pre-posing without a detached pronoun highlights the object without excluding alternatives.

recognition_criteria: a detached accusative pronoun stands before the verb
the verb has no clitic object of its own filling the same role
an alternative is negated or contrasted in the immediate context
a full noun in the accusative is followed by a matching detached pronoun before the verb
the reading available is this one and not another rather than merely this one
procedures: determine that the object is to be placed before the verb
select the detached accusative pronoun matching the referent in person, gender and number
place it before the verb rather than attaching it
optionally pre-pose the full noun first and echo it with the detached pronoun
add an explicit negation of the alternative where the exclusive reading is to be made unambiguous
conditions: the pronoun must be in the detached accusative series to occupy pre-verbal position
the pronoun must agree with its referent in person, gender and number
the exclusive reading is supported by contrast or explicit negation of alternatives
exceptions: not every pre-posing yields exclusion; ordinary pre-posing may only emphasise
restriction can also be achieved without pre-posing by a restrictive particle or by negation plus exception
the dual member of the series is shared between masculine and feminine referents
contrasts: clitic object in place against detached pronoun pre-posed
emphasis without exclusion against exclusion of alternatives
pre-posing as a restriction device against a restrictive particle against negation plus exception
a plain statement carrying no restriction against any of the restriction devices

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading every pre-posed object as exclusive.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Pre-posing on its own may only emphasise; exclusion is signalled by the detached pronoun or by explicit contrast.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Look for the detached pronoun or for a negated alternative before asserting an exclusive reading.

common_mistakes.pattern: Attempting to place a clitic pronoun in pre-verbal position.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Clitics cannot be detached from their host and cannot open a clause.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Switch to the detached accusative series whenever the pronoun must precede the verb.

common_mistakes.pattern: Selecting a detached pronoun whose gender or number does not match the referent.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The pronoun stands for the referent and inherits its features.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Resolve the referent's features first, then select the series member.

common_mistakes.pattern: Understanding the exclusive construction as merely additive, as though other objects were still included.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The construction is taught as narrowing the action to the named object and away from all others.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Render the exclusive reading explicitly when translating or glossing.

assuming pre-posing always yields restriction rather than, in some analyses, heightened attention without exclusion
treating the several restriction devices as freely interchangeable when they differ in what they presuppose about the alternative
generalising from one celebrated scriptural example to all pre-posed objects

instructional_purpose: Teaches the construction in which a pronoun is narrowed by an accusative noun naming the group it refers to, explains the accusative through an estimated verb of specifying, and shows how the pattern is used to claim collective identity.
concepts_taught: the specification construction (أسلوب الاختصاص)
the three-part structure of pronoun, specifying noun and predicate
accusative on the specifier licensed by an estimated verb meaning I specify or I mean
the variant introduced by أيّها or أيّتها in which the noun is nominative

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A pronoun may be narrowed by a following noun that names the group it refers to.
The specifying noun stands in the accusative.
The accusative is licensed by an estimated unpronounced verb meaning I specify or I mean.
In the variant introduced by أيّها or أيّتها the following noun is nominative instead.
The nominative in that variant is explained by treating the sequence as a vocative structure with a declined addressed noun.
The specifying noun must be definite, whether by the article, by construct annexation or as a proper name.
An indefinite accusative specifier is also possible though uncommon.
The construction is available with a second-person pronoun as well as with the first person.
The construction differs from the vocative in that the speaker is inside the named group rather than addressing it.
The pronoun itself remains the topic and the following predicate remains the comment.

recognition_criteria: an independent pronoun opens the clause
a definite noun in the accusative follows it immediately
that noun names a group of which the pronoun is a member
a predicate follows and agrees with the pronoun, not with the specifying noun
the specifying noun is not itself the subject of the predicate
procedures: place the independent pronoun first
select the noun naming the group and make it definite
mark it accusative, or introduce it with the vocative-like particle and mark it nominative in that variant
supply the predicate agreeing with the pronoun
when parsing, name the estimated verb that licenses the accusative
conditions: the specifier must be definite in the standard pattern
the specifier must name a group containing the pronoun's referent
the case depends on which of the two patterns is used, accusative in the bare pattern and nominative after the introducing particle
exceptions: the introducing-particle variant reverses the expected case
an indefinite specifier is presented as marginal and is elsewhere in the same lesson treated as incorrect
second-person use is admitted, extending beyond the first-person default
contrasts: the bare accusative pattern against the introducing-particle nominative pattern
specification against the vocative
specification against ordinary apposition, where both nouns share one case
a plain predication against the same predication with the group named

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving the specifying noun in the nominative in the bare pattern.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: An estimated verb of specifying governs it and assigns the accusative.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Recover the estimated governor before assigning case.

common_mistakes.pattern: Marking the noun accusative after the introducing particle.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In that variant the noun follows a vocative-like element and surfaces in the nominative.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let the presence of the introducing particle decide the case.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using an indefinite noun as the specifier.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The standard pattern requires a definite noun; the indefinite version is at best marginal.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Definite the specifier by article, annexation or proper name.

common_mistakes.pattern: Analysing the sequence as ordinary apposition.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Apposition matches the case of its head and follows a noun directly, while this construction interrupts a pronoun and its predicate and carries its own case.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Compare cases across the two nouns and check whether a predicate is being interrupted.

explaining the introducing-particle variant purely as a vocative, which obscures that the speaker is not addressing the group
assuming free availability with any person of the pronoun when the first-person plural is the settled case and other persons are contested
treating the estimated verb as recoverable material that could simply be inserted

instructional_purpose: Teaches two verbless exhortation patterns, one urging a hearer toward a quality and one warning a hearer away from something, both realised as bare accusative nouns licensed by an unpronounced imperative.
concepts_taught: the encouragement construction (الإغراء)
the warning construction (التحذير)
the estimated imperative meaning adhere to as licenser for encouragement
the estimated imperative meaning beware as licenser for warning
single, repeated and coordinated forms of the bare accusative
the detached-pronoun plus conjunction pattern characteristic of warning
the variant using a subordinator plus subjunctive verb
person selection on the detached pronoun including self-directed and first-person-plural warnings
the register and pragmatic force of verbless exhortation

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A bare accusative noun can function as an exhortation urging adherence to the quality it names.
A bare accusative noun can function as a warning away from what it names.
The accusative in both is licensed by an unpronounced transitive imperative, adhere to for encouragement and beware for warning.
The exhortation may be a single noun, the same noun repeated, or two nouns joined by the conjunction.
The characteristic warning pattern is a detached accusative pronoun followed by the conjunction and an accusative noun.
The conjunction is obligatory in that pattern and omitting it is an error.
A warning can also be framed as the detached pronoun followed by a subordinator and a subjunctive verb.
The detached pronoun must agree with the addressee, including self-directed and inclusive first-person-plural uses.
The nominative is never available in either construction.
The two constructions are distinguished by the polarity of what is named, positive qualities for encouragement and negative ones for warning.

recognition_criteria: a bare accusative noun stands as a complete utterance with no visible verb
the noun names a quality or a danger rather than an entity in a predication
the noun may be repeated or paired with a second accusative noun
a detached accusative pronoun is followed by the conjunction and an accusative noun
the surrounding discourse is advisory, hortatory or admonitory
procedures: decide whether the target is to be pursued or avoided
for encouragement, place the quality in the accusative alone, repeated, or paired with a second accusative noun
for warning, either place the danger in the accusative alone or use the detached pronoun matching the addressee, then the conjunction, then the accusative noun
alternatively frame the warning with the subordinator and a subjunctive verb
when parsing, name the estimated imperative that licenses the accusative
conditions: the noun must be accusative in both constructions
the detached pronoun must match the addressee in person, gender and number
the conjunction is required between the detached pronoun and the noun in the characteristic warning pattern
exceptions: the detached-pronoun pattern belongs to warning only and does not serve encouragement
some warnings dispense with the pronoun entirely and use only a repeated or single accusative noun
the subordinator variant replaces the noun with a verbal clause
contrasts: encouragement against warning by polarity and by estimated licenser
bare accusative noun against detached pronoun plus conjunction
repetition for emphasis against coordination of two qualities
verbless exhortation against an explicit imperative or prohibition

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving the exhorted noun in the nominative.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The estimated imperative is transitive and assigns the accusative to its object.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Recover the estimated imperative and mark its object accusative.

common_mistakes.pattern: Omitting the conjunction between the detached pronoun and the noun in the warning pattern.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In the pattern as taught, both the pronoun and the noun are objects of the estimated imperative and the conjunction links them.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Keep the conjunction in the canonical pattern.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using the warning pattern to urge a positive quality.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: That pattern encodes avoidance, so applying it to a virtue reverses the intended message.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Match the pattern to the polarity of the intended exhortation.

common_mistakes.pattern: Choosing a detached pronoun that does not match the addressee.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The pronoun identifies who is being warned and must agree with that person.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Resolve the addressee first, then select the pronoun.

misleading_shortcuts: treating the conjunction as universally obligatory when other warning frames without it are attested in the tradition
assuming any bare accusative in isolation is one of these constructions rather than an ellipsis of some other kind
assuming the estimated imperative may never be pronounced, when overt versions of the same exhortation exist and are simply outside these named patterns
reading the detached pronoun as the target of the warning in every case, when it can also be self-directed or inclusive

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A small class of verbs governs three accusative complements.
These verbs are causative counterparts of verbs that themselves take two accusative complements.
The first complement names the person made to know or perceive.
The second and third complements correspond to the two complements of the underlying non-causative verb, the third predicating a state of the second.
All three complements carry accusative marking.
The person complement must precede the content complement.
The third complement may be dropped, after which the verb behaves like an ordinary two-complement verb.
A complement may be realised as a clitic on the verb or as a detached accusative pronoun.
The listed verbs share the meaning of causing someone to know or perceive something in a certain state.
The causative counterparts are formed transparently from their bases.

recognition_criteria: the verb belongs to the listed informing or showing class
three accusative-marked constituents follow it, or two follow a clitic that counts as the first
the first constituent denotes an animate recipient of knowledge
the third constituent is predicable of the second
removing the third leaves a coherent two-complement clause
procedures: identify the verb and confirm class membership
assign the first complement to the person informed or shown
assign the second complement to the content
assign the third complement to the state predicated of the content
mark all three accusative
check that the person complement precedes the content complement
note where a complement is realised by a clitic or by a detached pronoun

the ordering with the person first is fixed
all three complements require accusative marking
exceptions: the third complement may be omitted, reducing the frame
a complement may surface as a bound clitic rather than as a full noun
a complement may surface as a detached accusative pronoun where a second clitic cannot attach
contrasts: one-complement transitives against two-complement mental-state verbs against three-complement causatives
the non-causative base verb against its causative counterpart
correct person-first ordering against the reversed ordering
the full three-complement frame against the reduced two-complement use

common_mistakes.pattern: Placing the content complement before the person complement.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The frame fixes the person made to know as the first complement.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Order the complements by role, not by salience.

common_mistakes.pattern: Omitting the third complement while still intending the full three-complement reading.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Without it the clause reports only that someone was informed of something, not the state attributed to it.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Retain the third complement whenever the attributed state is part of the message.

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving any complement in the nominative.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: All three positions are governed by the verb and take the accusative.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Apply accusative marking uniformly across all three positions.
